episode_title: Smarter gene tokens for single-cell models, agentic drug-response simulators, and how cell division writes noise into gene expression

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Morning. It's Thursday, November fifth. Looks like about twenty seven new preprints landed across the archive and the bio-archive overnight.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And today's a good one for the methods crowd. We've got a rethink of how single-cell foundation models tokenize transcriptomes, an agentic system that tries to predict, explain, and revise its own calls about drug responses, a deep review on how cell growth and division shape expression noise, and agents that build whole virtual tissue simulations by themselves.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Let's get into it. Paper one in the show notes is about single-cell foundation models, and it's attacking a pretty basic design choice: one gene equals one token.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Right, and that choice is expensive. A cell can express thousands of genes, so if every detected gene gets its own token, self-attention cost blows up fast. The catch is that a lot of those tokens carry almost no signal because the gene's barely expressed.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So what did they actually change?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They built something called S-C-TAT, short for transcriptome aware tokenization. Instead of only a vocabulary of single genes, they add a vocabulary of overlapping gene sets, groups of genes that tend to co-vary with stable relative expression across the pretraining data. Then, for each individual cell, a tokenizer decides on the fly whether a group of genes should collapse into one shared token, or whether a gene is distinctive enough to earn its own token.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: How do you even compare a multi-gene token to a single-gene token on the same footing?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: They score each candidate, set or single gene, by its expression, normalized by the square root of the set size, and the highest scoring candidates win token positions. Even though tokens can bundle several genes, the model still has to reconstruct expression at individual gene resolution during training, so you don't lose gene-level granularity.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: And does it actually help?

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: In frozen embedding cell type annotation, scTAT matches the strongest one gene per token model while using half the token budget. The gap in its favor grows as the token budget shrinks, because that's exactly when it leans harder on gene sets to cover more of the transcriptome. It also nearly halves the transformer's matrix multiplication cost for the same gene coverage.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: So basically a smarter compression scheme rather than a new architecture.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Exactly, no accuracy cost, same model, just rethinking what counts as one unit of input. For anyone fine-tuning these single-cell foundation models on a budget, that's a very practical result.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper two is CellCanon, which bills itself as an agentic cellular world model.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Agentic is doing a lot of work in that sentence. What's the actual problem?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Predicting how single cells respond to a drug or genetic perturbation is already a well studied task, but most models just spit out a number. CellCanon tries to also explain its predictions with evidence it can point to, and update its beliefs when new measurements come in, without retraining.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: How does it do prediction and explanation together?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: There's a shared world state linking three things: the predictions, newly acquired measurements, and claims tied back to their biological source. The predictive core reuses condition level biological evidence, things known about the drug or pathway, to help generate gene specific single cell expression predictions, and the explanation and revision steps read from that same shared state.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What did they test it on?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Three hundred thirty nine held out conditions from SciPlex three, a drug perturbation screen, across three cell lines. Against the best baseline for each metric, CellCanon improves differential expression A-U-P-R-C by sixty three point three percent, macro F-one by seventeen point three percent, and gets the direction of change right more often too, a gain of seven point two percent in direction macro F-one.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: There's a big efficiency claim buried in there as well.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, compared to just asking a language model to reason gene by gene, CellCanon cuts token usage by over ninety nine percent for prediction and over ninety eight percent for explanation. On a benchmark checking whether its explanations are grounded in real sources, it answers every answerable question correctly with supporting evidence, and correctly flags the cases where there isn't enough evidence.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the updating part?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: In a simulated feedback loop, given one new measured data point per drug, it beats fine tuned baselines on differential expression metrics without changing any model weights. The honest caveat is that all of this is on one perturbation screen, so how the explanation and update machinery generalizes beyond SciPlex three is still open. But as a design pattern, coupling prediction with traceable evidence and cheap revision is appealing for anyone trying to use these models iteratively in a wet lab loop.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper three is a review from Ramon Grima's group on modeling gene expression noise, and it's squarely about something every single-cell person runs into: why do m-R-N-A counts vary so much cell to cell, and what model do you fit to a count distribution?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The standard answer has been the telegraph model, a gene switching between on and off states, or the simpler bursty model, which fit single cell count distributions reasonably well and let people estimate burst size and frequency.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What's the issue with those?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They all treat the cell as static, as if it just sits there transcribing with constant kinetics. This review covers models that build in the cell's actual life history, birth, DNA replication, and division, and ask how that history leaves its own signature on m-R-N-A and protein number distributions.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So gene expression noise and cell cycle effects are genuinely tangled together.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Right, and the review works through what's called cyclo-stationary behavior, the idea that in a growing, dividing population a gene's expression statistics settle into a repeating pattern tied to the cell cycle rather than a single steady state. They discuss when that cyclo-stationary behavior is well approximated by the steady state of the simpler static models, and when it isn't.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: That matters for interpretation, since people fit static models to single cell snapshots all the time.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Exactly, and the review goes into that directly, how the distributions you measure depend sensitively on the experimental setup, snapshot sequencing versus lineage tracking versus live imaging, and how to fit these dynamic models to real single cell data. They also cover separating genuine biological variability from measurement noise, and what computational tricks make it feasible to fit these richer models across thousands of genes rather than one at a time.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Any big open problems flagged?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The abstract just says they close with the field's open problems without listing specifics. Given the authors, I'd guess scaling cyclo-stationary inference genome-wide and handling extrinsic noise jointly with cell cycle structure are in there. Worth reading before trusting a static telegraph model fit on scRNA-seq data.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper four is a short one, Morpheus dot A-I, about large language model agents that build virtual tissue models on their own.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Virtual tissue models being multicellular simulations, things like cellular Potts models, that link observations to a mechanistic hypothesis. Normally building one needs real expertise in biology, math, and programming all at once.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What did the agents actually do?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: They paired a frontier large language model with the simulator Morpheus and set it loose on fifteen benchmark studies, five of which didn't even have a published model to copy from. The agents wrote and refined the simulation code themselves, ran it, checked it against the study's criteria, and iterated.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And how good were the results?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Across those fifteen studies, the agent-built models met eighty three to eighty six percent of the study-specific success criteria, in under two hours and under four U-S dollars per model.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Striking cost and speed numbers. What's the catch, given this is a short abstract?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: We don't get detail on what those success criteria actually measure, so it's hard to judge whether eighty three percent means the model nails the core biology or just gets the broad shape right. It's also a nice test case for agent autonomy generally, since tissue modeling has clear, checkable criteria, unlike a lot of open-ended biology questions. If it holds up, it points toward in silico tissue modeling becoming something you generate and test automatically, rather than something that needs a dedicated modeler for weeks.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper five, VenusGenome, is about representation learning for microbial genomes, building on protein language model embeddings but adding genomic context.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: The starting observation is simple: a gene's protein embedding is partly predictable just from the embeddings of its neighbors in the genome. Genes sitting together often function together, operons and so on. So they push that idea into a masked autoencoder trained with a high masking ratio, forcing the model to reconstruct a gene's embedding from a sparse set of surrounding genes.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Why does the masking ratio matter so much here?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Because genomic context brings its own artifacts. If a genome was assembled from short reads, two genes on different contigs aren't necessarily close biologically, and strand labels only make sense relative to an arbitrary reference orientation. So VenusGenome uses genome-aware attention that explicitly encodes contig boundaries, relative strand orientation, and gene position, rather than assuming a naive linear order.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: What did they train it on?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: A curated set of over one point seven million microbial genome assemblies, both cultured isolates and metagenomic assemblies, using frozen protein embeddings as the gene-level input features, so the genome model sits on top of an existing protein embedding model rather than learning sequence from scratch.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And the payoff?

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: On a mix of genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the frozen VenusGenome representations come out on top on nine of eleven primary metrics against the comparison models. A gene-input perturbation analysis also found that how sensitive a gene's representation is to perturbation lines up with experimentally measured fitness defects, a nice independent sanity check. Ablations confirm the genome-aware attention is pulling weight, and that masked autoencoding with high masking ratios beats a more standard BERT-style masking scheme.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: So less about single genes, more about treating the genome as a sequence with its own grammar, a bit like how enhancer grammar gets learned from chromatin accessibility, just one level up, from regulatory elements to gene neighborhoods.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's the deep dives. A few more worth a quick mention.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper six proposes a training-free way to plug a D-N-A foundation model into a frozen large language model. Instead of training a connector, they fit a single ridge regression mapping frozen Evo two features onto the host model's own representation of a gene's name and description, then splice that in at an early layer. On a five-way gene identity benchmark, real D-N-A reliably beats shuffled D-N-A across four different host language models, and a layer-selection rule picked without any task data correctly predicted which layer would work on a model it hadn't seen yet.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper seven gives a system-theoretic treatment of cellular Potts models extended with extracellular matrix degradation, used to study tumor invasion. They recast the model as a stochastic process for interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system for the matrix, and in one-dimensional settings derive closed-form expressions for how long invasion takes as a function of the matrix gradient, cell number, and each cell's tendency to hold its target volume.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper eight, called Pev, is a general mutation policy for protein engineering, trained across many protein families rather than one target family at a time. Given a parent sequence, it returns calibrated probabilities for which edit to try next or whether to stop, in a single pass rather than scoring each candidate separately. In held-out family screens it finds three times as many beneficial mutations as random choice, and almost twice as many as zero-shot E-S-M-two.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper nine, BIOTRAM, tackles a problem anyone doing metabarcoding knows: raw read counts from bulk arthropod samples don't track true relative abundance, because D-N-A yield and amplification efficiency differ by species and body size. Their neural network learns a per-taxon read yield to correct for that, and on a large paired dataset with ground-truth individual barcoding, it substantially cuts the divergence between estimated and true composition compared to using raw read proportions, and it generalizes better to new regions, dates, and sequencing batches than generic deep learning baselines.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper ten is more origin-of-life theory than wet-lab biology, a stochastic model of how self-sustaining, reflexively autocatalytic reaction networks can emerge from a handful of catalysts. The interesting result is that when catalytic strength is heavy-tailed, these self-sustaining networks can emerge with probability approaching one even as the average catalytic intensity goes to zero, which breaks the classical phase-transition picture.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper eleven asks a pointed question about clinical trial simulators: do they actually use information about which drug was given, or are they just pattern matching on other trial features? Testing a registry-trained model against a version with the intervention hidden, the standard gradient-boosting simulator gets worse, not better, when told the drug, meaning its apparent accuracy has nothing to do with drug effects. A large language model reading the trial protocol text does show some real, if modest, sensitivity to which intervention was used.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper twelve, AgentCount, is an agentic pipeline for counting bacterial colonies on agar plates, chaining image quality control, plate detection, segmentation with a general-purpose vision model, and a language-model agent that writes up the results narrative. Checked against two previously published microbiology datasets, its colony counts agreed with the published values to within a tight tolerance on the vast majority of replicate measurements.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper thirteen compares a convolutional network reading thyroid ultrasound images against molecular testing for indeterminate thyroid nodules. In their held-out test set the imaging model was more specific and had a better positive predictive value than the molecular test, though with lower sensitivity, and combining the two didn't beat the imaging model alone, a reminder that a more expensive test doesn't automatically add information.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper fourteen applies conformal prediction to Parkinsonian diagnosis using Canadian registry data, where three quarters of predictor fields are typically missing. Single-label prediction did poorly on the rare atypical Parkinsonian group, but conformal prediction sets, and combining multiple models into a list, pushed coverage of the correct diagnosis up to around ninety nine percent, at the cost of slightly longer candidate lists for patients with the most missing data.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper fifteen compares Bayesian superpopulation models for estimating type one diabetes prevalence from multi-site electronic health records that aren't a representative sample of the population. Of the three approaches tested, a simple analysis-of-variance style model held up best under simulation, while the more popular multilevel regression and poststratification approach degraded badly with smaller samples or more complex selection bias.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: And a quick round-up of the rest. Paper sixteen frames language model reasoning length as a competing-risks problem, splitting outcomes into right, wrong, or running out of token budget. Paper seventeen gives an exact Poisson mixture representation of remaining life expectancy under the Siler mortality model. Paper eighteen develops efficient estimation for recurrent-event regression when a terminal event like death can cut the recurrent process short.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: Paper nineteen proposes a latent-space hidden Markov model for clustering different views of longitudinal multilayer networks. Paper twenty introduces an exponential seniority weighting scheme for chain-ladder insurance reserving. Paper twenty-one argues that picking marketing mix models by predictive fit alone can mislead, and proposes validating against experimental return-on-ad-spend benchmarks instead.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: Paper twenty-two speeds up Gaussian process modeling for large, replicated, and censored industrial datasets. Paper twenty-three builds a decision framework for F-D-I-C assisted distressed bank acquisitions, using the Silicon Valley Bank case as an example. Paper twenty-four introduces a multimodal benchmark for generative models in the acupuncture domain. And paper twenty-five looks at whether simple, predictable strategies beat optimizing for volatility when households try to save on fuel costs.

segments.speaker: Ava
segments.text: That's today's set. A lot of representation learning on genomes this morning, from gene tokens to microbial genome context.

segments.speaker: Leo
segments.text: See you tomorrow.

picks.title: Rethinking One Gene, One Token: Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization for Single-Cell Foundation Models
picks.abstract: Single-cell foundation models typically treat each gene as a token, which is both costly and wasteful. A cell can express thousands of genes, so one token per gene makes self-attention expensive, yet many of these genes are detected at low levels and carry too little signal to deserve a token of their own. Genes that are expressed together could instead share a token, leaving separate tokens for genes that stand out. We introduce scTAT (Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization), which pairs a gene-set vocabulary with a per-cell tokenizer. The vocabulary holds overlapping gene sets that recur with stable relative expression across the pretraining corpus. Using these sets raises two difficulties. First, which genes should share a token depends on the cell, whereas existing multi-gene tokens fix the grouping in advance. Second, gene sets of different sizes must be compared with single genes on a common scale. The tokenizer therefore decides per cell, letting gene sets and single genes compete for token positions under an expression score normalized by the square root of set size. Training still reconstructs individual genes, so predictions stay at gene resolution. In frozen-embedding cell-type annotation, scTAT matches the strongest one-gene-per-token model with half the token budget. Its advantage over one-gene-per-token models at the same budget grows as the budget shrinks and the tokenizer assigns more positions to gene sets. Encoding the same genes with gene-set tokens also nearly halves the Transformer's matrix-multiplication cost. These results show that a token need not hold exactly one gene: when the tokenizer decides per cell which genes share a token, a fixed budget covers more of each transcriptome at no cost in annotation accuracy.
picks.why: Proposes gene-set tokenization for single-cell foundation models that halves compute while matching annotation accuracy, directly tackling a core scalability bottleneck in scRNA-seq modeling.

picks.title: CellCanon: An Agentic Cellular World Model for Prediction, Explanation, and Observation-Driven Updating
picks.abstract: Biological discovery requires using molecular knowledge and new measurements to infer responses beyond the conditions already observed. We introduce CellCanon, the first agentic cellular world model to unify single-cell expression prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and observation-driven updating. Its predictive core reuses condition-level biological evidence across gene-specific numerical readouts to guide single-cell expression generation. A shared world state links predictions, acquired measurements, and source-linked claims, supporting explanation and revision. On 339 held-out SciPlex3 conditions across three cell lines, CellCanon improves differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 over the best baseline for each metric by 63.3% and 17.3%, respectively, and direction Macro-F1 by 7.2%. Relative to gene-wise reasoning on matched drug-cell cohorts, measured language-model token use falls by 99.77% for Predict and 98.41% for Explain. On the source-grounded benchmark, Explain correctly answers all answerable questions with supporting proofs and identifies all insufficient-evidence cases. In simulated experimental feedback, Update uses one measured source context per drug to exceed the best fine-tuned baselines in differential-expression AUPRC and Macro-F1 without changing model weights. Together, these capabilities support a cumulative account of cellular responses, with predictions and biological judgments that can be revised as evidence accumulates.
picks.why: CellCanon's agentic world model unifies single-cell perturbation prediction, evidence-grounded explanation, and iterative updating, substantially beating baselines on SciPlex3 differential expression tasks.

picks.title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
picks.abstract: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.
picks.why: A comprehensive review connecting stochastic gene expression models (telegraph/bursty) to cell growth and division dynamics, essential synthesis for anyone modeling transcriptional noise mechanistically.

picks.title: Morpheus.AI: agents autonomously generate, execute and refine virtual tissue models
picks.abstract: Virtual tissue models link observations to mechanistic hypotheses, but building them demands expertise in biology, mathematics and programming. Here, large language model (LLM) agents paired with the simulator Morpheus (Morpheus.AI) autonomously built such models from fifteen benchmark studies, five without a published model. With a frontier LLM, agents that ran their simulations met 83-86% of study-specific criteria in under two hours and for under US\$4 per model. Such agents could make in silico modeling routine.
picks.why: LLM agents autonomously build and validate mechanistic virtual tissue models from benchmark studies in under two hours, pointing to a new paradigm for systems biology model construction.

picks.title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
picks.abstract: Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.
picks.why: VenusGenome's genome-aware masked autoencoder incorporating contig and strand structure sets a new standard for microbial genome representation learning across phenotype and gene-level tasks.

picks.title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
picks.abstract: Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host. We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points. A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.
picks.why: A training-free ridge-regression 'socket' lets frozen LLMs incorporate DNA foundation model (Evo 2) features for gene-level QA without any gradient-based connector training.

picks.title: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion
picks.abstract: The Cellular Potts Model has emerged as a standard framework for modeling multicellular systems and metastatic progression. Yet, computational extensions incorporating cell movement within spatial gradients of Extracellular Matrix (ECM), an important element of the tissue microenvironment, lack theoretical foundations. This work provides a system-theoretic formulation and analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models (ECPMs) that explicitly couple tumor dynamics with ECM degradation. We reformulate the ECPM as an interconnected dynamical system: a stochastic process describing a network of locally interacting tumor cells coupled to a jump-linear system describing ECM evolution. By exploiting the sparse energy structure of the model, we characterize asymptotic ECM behavior, transition probabilities with uniform bounds, and global system convergence. In one-dimensional settings, we derive closed-form expressions for invasion time probabilities, revealing how mean invasion time depends on local ECM gradients, number of cells and their tendency to maintain a target volume. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions, establishing a principled foundation for analyzing haptotaxis-driven invasion in Potts-based models.
picks.why: Provides a rigorous system-theoretic analysis of extended Cellular Potts Models coupling tumor cell dynamics with ECM degradation, deriving closed-form invasion time predictions relevant to cancer invasion modeling.

picks.title: A System One Approach to General Protein Evolution
picks.abstract: Protein engineering requires deciding which mutation to test next and when to stop. Existing approaches often require target-family measurements, encode candidates separately, or return scores that are not calibrated to the assay. We introduce Pev, a general mutation policy that explores a System One approach to protein evolution: learning from experiments across families to make decisions in a single parallel query. Given a parent sequence and an assay context, Pev encodes the parent once and returns calibrated probabilities for choosing an edit or stopping, together with each edit's probability of improving the assay outcome. One policy covers peptides, small folded domains, and antibodies across binding and stability objectives, without fitting model weights to the target family. In ten-well screens on held-out families, Pev finds 3.3\times as many beneficial mutations as random selection and 1.8\times as many as zero-shot ESM-2. It also outperforms a ridge surrogate refitted on target measurements in closed-loop search on the held-out GB1 landscape. Post-hoc calibration improves probability reliability without changing decisions, while shared encoding provides over 800\times the throughput of per-mutant encoding at 1,000 candidates per request. These results suggest that a System One approach could support efficient experimental decisions across protein families, with Pev providing an initial demonstration.
picks.why: Pev introduces a cross-family mutation policy for protein engineering that triples the hit rate of random mutagenesis in held-out family screens without target-specific retraining.

picks.title: BIOTRAM: Biochemistry-informed Transformer for Relative Abundance via Metabarcoding
picks.abstract: Arthropod monitoring at scale begins with metabarcoding of bulk samples: trap collections of hundreds to thousands of specimens processed as one unit, extraction of DNA from the bulked specimens, then sequencing of the DNA from all specimens together. Metabarcoding reveals which taxa such a sample contains, but due to factors such as differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, its read counts do not neatly correspond to how abundant the different taxa are relative to one another. This lack of relative abundance limits the data's utility for the multitude of ecological analyses that depend on it. We propose BIOTRAM: a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts by dividing the observed read counts by a learned read yield per specimen, which it factors into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified. On a paired dataset of 1,188 bottles (800 k specimens) processed both by metabarcoding and by comprehensive individual barcoding for ground-truthing, BIOTRAM reduces the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the estimated and the true composition from 0.3586 for raw read proportions (the usual proxy for abundance) to 0.1200. Trained on the same objective and inputs as four generic deep architectures, all with tuned loss weights, it reaches a count error 3.2% below that of the strongest of them and the lowest composition divergence. It also generalizes to out-of-domain data better, beating all baselines on bottles from unseen regions, later collection dates and unseen sequencing batches, and transferring to data from an unseen laboratory. Structuring the mapping from reads to counts around the steps of the experimental pipeline thus yields more accurate abundance estimates than leaving that mapping unconstrained.
picks.why: BIOTRAM models the biochemical steps of metabarcoding (DNA yield and amplification efficiency per specimen) to convert noisy read counts into much more accurate relative abundance estimates.

picks.title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
picks.abstract: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.
picks.why: A rigorous stochastic extension of RAF-set theory shows that heavy-tailed catalytic activity can allow self-sustaining chemical networks to emerge even as catalytic intensity vanishes, a notable origin-of-life result.

picks.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials
picks.abstract: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.
picks.why: A large-scale audit of clinical trial simulators finds that a standard gradient-boosting model's predictive accuracy comes almost entirely from non-causal correlations rather than genuine knowledge of the intervention tested.

picks.title: AgentCount: An Agentic Workflow for Traceable Colony Counting and Insight Generation from Agar Plate Images
picks.abstract: Colony counting is commonly used to evaluate microbial populations in food safety testing and microbiological studies. Despite its wide application, manual counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often lacks a record of the objects included in the measurement. To address these limitations, this study presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images. Plate photographs and plating metadata are processed through seven agents for image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation, and reporting. Colony detection is performed using Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering. After that, replicate statistics are calculated and a large language model (LLM)-based agent is used to generate a results narrative. Intermediate outputs, including quality scores, segmentation masks, detections, and warnings, are retained to support review of the reported values. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data. In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, we benchmarked 241 published endpoints, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. Overall, AgentCount demonstrates the promising potential of agentic workflows for applications in applied microbiology.
picks.why: AgentCount combines SAM-3 segmentation with an LLM-reporting pipeline for traceable, auditable colony counting, matching published microbiology benchmarks to within 0.01 log10 units.

picks.title: Deep-Learning Algorithm for Indeterminate Thyroid Nodules: Comparison and Combination with Molecular Testing
picks.abstract: Thyroid nodules with indeterminate cytology (Bethesda III) carry an intermediate risk of malignancy, and molecular testing is widely used to decide between surgery and surveillance, but it is costly and not universally available. We investigated whether a convolutional neural network (CNN) applied to routine ultrasound images can stratify Bethesda III nodules, and how it compares and combines with molecular testing. We retrospectively identified 466 nodule records from 418 patients who underwent molecular testing (Afirma or ThyroSeq). A CNN pre-trained on determinate nodules was adapted to indeterminate nodules with soft labels and transfer learning. After removal of duplicate records, 119 nodules with surgical pathology were used for development and 47 were held out for testing. On the test set, the deep learning (DL) model achieved an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI 0.51-0.94), compared with 0.55 (0.38-0.71) for molecular testing (P = 0.15). At a cut-off inherited from the original algorithm, the DL model was more specific than molecular testing (0.95 vs 0.32; P < 0.001), with a higher positive predictive value (0.67 vs 0.21), a lower sensitivity (0.44 vs 0.78; P = 0.25) and a similar negative predictive value (0.88 vs 0.86). All six DL-positive test nodules were molecular-positive, and the DL output split the molecular-positive nodules into a high-risk (4/6 malignant) and a lower-risk group (3/27 malignant; P = 0.01). Surgical verification was strongly driven by the molecular result (99% of positive vs 19% of negative results), and molecular-test accuracy depended on the platform. A logistic regression of the DL output, nodule size and the molecular result dropped the DL term and did not improve on the DL output alone. Ultrasound DL complemented molecular testing for Bethesda III nodules, in particular by identifying molecular-positive nodules at lower risk of malignancy.
picks.why: A CNN on routine ultrasound images stratifies indeterminate thyroid nodules with higher specificity than costly molecular testing, suggesting a complementary low-cost triage tool.

picks.title: Uncertainty aware prediction from incomplete clinical records: a conformal prediction study of Parkinsonian classification using C-OPN data
authors: for the Canadian Open Parkinson Network
picks.abstract: Background: Incomplete clinical records and imbalanced diagnostic groups complicate Parkinsonian classification. We examined whether incomplete records could support useful lists of diagnostic possibilities through conformal prediction, assessing how often the lists retained the recorded diagnosis, their length and the uncertainty remaining. Methods: We analyzed records from 3,434 Canadian Open Parkinson Network participants: 2,853 with Parkinson's disease, 171 in the atypical Parkinsonian group (AP) and 410 healthy controls. In three repeats of five-fold cross-validation, we compared single-category predictions, conformal prediction sets and lists combined across 21 analyses using alternative models and assumptions about missing entries. An information deficit score summarized unavailable information. Results: The median proportion of eligible predictor entries unrecorded per participant was 75.6%. Single-category prediction correctly classified 89.29% of test records (balanced accuracy 55.40%), but only 10.33% of AP records. Conformal prediction sets included the recorded category in 93.35% of evaluation records and averaged 1.846 categories; combined lists increased inclusion to approximately 99% and averaged 2.289 categories. AP inclusion increased from 98.05% to 100%. Combined lists averaged 1.010 more categories in the group with the greatest information deficit than in the group with the least (95% interval 0.996-1.023). Conclusions: Even with extensive missing information and imbalanced diagnostic groups, clinical records can support informative prediction when uncertainty is quantified and expressed through sets of possible diagnoses rather than a single label. Joint assessment of list length and information deficit showed both the narrowing achieved and the records for which all three categories remained open.
picks.why: Conformal prediction on heavily incomplete Parkinsonian clinical records yields diagnostic sets with ~99% coverage, showing how uncertainty quantification can salvage decision support from sparse data.

picks.title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data
picks.abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) are increasingly used for disease surveillance. However, data collected in EHRs may not be a representative sample of the target population for inference. Methods for EHR-based surveillance remain in their nascence. In addition to simple weighting approaches, researchers have used multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), a popular technique for finite population quantity estimation that remains understudied in EHRs. We are motivated by a US-based collaborative to modernize diabetes surveillance using EHR data from different health system centers across the country. To estimate type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence in children and adolescents, we propose and evaluate three Bayesian superpopulation models that are distinguished by how they account for two important features of EHR data: unobserved heterogeneity and data sparsity. The three models include an analysis of variance-inspired approach; a model with geographic effects varying by demographic subgroup; and MRP, which we consider as the reference model. We apply the models to estimate prevalence overall and in demographic- and geographic-based subgroups. Using plasmode simulations, we evaluate model estimation performance while preserving the complexity of the EHR data. Our results show that the superpopulation-based prevalence estimates were higher than those observed in the EHR sample alone, with the magnitude of the differences varying by health system center. The bias and coverage probabilities of MRP markedly worsened when the EHR sample size was smaller or the selection mechanism was more complex. Overall, the superpopulation model based on analysis of variance demonstrated the best estimation performance.
picks.why: Compares Bayesian superpopulation models (including MRP) for correcting non-representative EHR sampling in diabetes surveillance, finding an ANOVA-style model most robust under sparse or complex selection.

picks.title: Right, Wrong, or Unfinished: A Competing Risks Framework for Language-Model Reasoning under Token Budgets
picks.abstract: Assessing language-model performance under a token budget requires understanding both when a response will finish and whether it will be correct. We develop Competing Risks Analysis of Token Expenditure in Reasoning (CRATER), a statistically principled framework that treats correct and incorrect completion as distinct competing event types and responses unfinished at the generation limit as administratively right-censored. The fitted distribution provides probabilities of correct completion, incorrect completion, and remaining unfinished across token budgets, together with expected token consumption. We evaluate the proposed method using responses to MATH questions and demonstrate its value in two downstream applications. For routing before generation, CRATER guides the joint choice of a model configuration and token budget. Under hypothetical token prices, it reduces mean cost by 53.39 \% relative to a strong reference, with observed correctcompletion rates of 96.42 \% and 97.30 \%, respectively. For repeated sampling, we combine CRATER's single-attempt success probabilities with an existing beta-binomial calibration approach to predict pass@k. Across both applications, CRATER delivers predictions at any specified token budget up to the generation limit from a common model of completion time and correctness, eliminating the need for separate parameter estimation for each budget.
picks.why: CRATER applies a competing-risks survival framework to predict whether and when LLM reasoning finishes correctly under a token budget, cutting inference costs by over half.

picks.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy
picks.abstract: The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. No standard closed form is available for its remaining life expectancy, which must therefore be evaluated by numerical integration. We show that Siler remaining life expectancy at age x is a Poisson mixture of Gompertz-Makeham remaining life expectancies, that is, a Poisson-weighted average of life expectancies in models with only a constant background hazard and an exponentially increasing senescence hazard. All components share the senescence hazard. Their background hazards increase from one component to the next by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines. The Poisson mean is the immaturity hazard that remains to be accumulated after age x. This representation yields an exact series of generalized exponential integrals with a closed-form bound on the truncation error. Replacing the background hazard by its discounted counterpart also gives the Laplace transform of the remaining lifetime. The mixture bounds the life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality: up to a term below the reciprocal of a2+b1, this loss equals the probability of an immaturity death times the life expectancy with the immaturity hazard removed. In annual Siler fits to Swedish female mortality, we estimate that the loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, which accounts for 15% of the gain in life expectancy at birth over the period.
picks.why: Derives an exact Poisson-mixture representation of life expectancy under the Siler mortality model, showing infant-mortality-driven life expectancy loss fell from 4.3 to under 0.01 years in Sweden since 1900.

picks.title: Efficient estimation of regression models for recurrent events in presence of terminal events
picks.abstract: Recurrent events are common in biomedical studies, and efficient methods are needed to analyse them, particularly when a terminal event may occur. Regression modelling of the marginal mean of recurrent events provides a simply interpretable approach, but standard estimation based on inverse probability of censoring weighting may not fully exploit observed event histories in multiple events settings. We demonstrate how the popular Ghosh-Lin proportional means model can be estimated efficiently by developing an augmentation procedure that is also applicable to composite endpoints. Using semiparametric efficiency theory, we characterize the fully efficient estimator. First, we investigate its construction under frailty models. We then propose a dynamic censoring-augmented estimator that is straightforward to compute and does not require a fully specified joint model for recurrent and terminal events. We show theoretically that it improves on the standard Ghosh-Lin estimator and derive an explicit expression for its asymptotic variance reduction. We also establish conditions under which tests of no treatment effect remain valid in randomized trials when the proportional means model is misspecified. Extensive simulations examine performance under dependence between recurrent and terminal events, unobserved heterogeneity, censoring-model misspecification, and auxiliary covariates. The practical gain of the proposed methods is illustrated with an analysis of catheter-related bloodstream infections in patients with chronic intestinal failure receiving home parenteral support.
picks.why: Develops a more statistically efficient augmented estimator for the Ghosh-Lin recurrent-events model when a terminal event can occur, with gains demonstrated on catheter infection data.

picks.title: A latent space hidden Markov model for clustering views in longitudinal multilayer networks
picks.abstract: We propose a Bayesian latent space model for clustering longitudinal multilayer networks in which network slices are represented by a finite set of recurrent latent regimes, each associated with a regime-specific latent geometric configuration. Layer-specific hidden Markov chains govern regime membership through a parsimonious additive transition model, allowing heterogeneous temporal dynamics across relational dimensions while sharing a common set of latent configurations. Edge weights are modelled using a Hurdle Negative Binomial distribution, accommodating both excess zeros and overdispersion in weighted networks. An optional sender-receiver extension further captures persistent node-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study demonstrates that the proposed model can accurately recover both latent regimes and their associated configurations, with recovery performance depending on the degree of regimes' similarity. We also assess the robustness of the proposed method under model misspecification. Applications to GDELT geopolitical event and European Parliament roll-call voting data demonstrate the flexibility of the framework across diverse domains.
picks.why: A Bayesian hidden Markov latent-space model clusters recurrent regimes in longitudinal multilayer networks, applied to geopolitical event and parliamentary voting data.

picks.title: Exponential Seniority Weighting Chain-Ladder Reserving
picks.abstract: We develop a tractable state-space version of the chain-ladder model. The state-space dynamics acts on the accident year axis which, in contrast to the classical chain-ladder model, makes accident years dependent. This state-space version yields an exponential seniority weighting in the chain-ladder factor estimation, and it admits an analytical likelihood representation that enables us to compute the seniority weighted chain-ladder reserves and their prediction uncertainty: the one-year uncertainty is available in closed form and the total uncertainty requires a Monte Carlo simulation from the fully tractable likelihood representation.
picks.why: Introduces a state-space chain-ladder variant for insurance reserving that yields exponential seniority weighting and closed-form uncertainty estimates.

picks.title: When Predictive Fit Misleads: Selecting Marketing Mix Models Using Experimental RoAS Benchmarks
picks.abstract: Marketing Mix Models (MMMs) are used to estimate channel-level Return on Ad Spend (RoAS) and guide marketing investment, yet competing specifications are usually compared on predictive-fit metrics such as out-of-sample R-squared, MAPE, or RMSE. We show that predictive fit can diverge from recovery of the causal quantities that drive marketing decisions. In simulations with known RoAS, the best-fitting specification is often not the one that recovers RoAS most accurately; replicated studies show that this disagreement is systematic and persists under media-spend collinearity, noise, and a misspecified carryover shape. Selecting specifications against experimental RoAS benchmarks, even imprecise ones, improves RoAS recovery relative to fit-based selection, and a real-world application with experimental benchmarks shows the same pattern. We propose an applied workflow: calibrate MMM specifications against estimand-aligned experimental benchmarks when they exist, and otherwise report RoAS sensitivity across plausible specifications rather than relying on a single best-fitting model.
picks.why: Shows that marketing mix models selected by predictive fit often fail to recover true causal ad-spend ROI, arguing for calibration against experimental benchmarks instead.

picks.title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research
picks.abstract: Gaussian process regression is widely used for modeling responses in both physical and computer experiments. In practice, data from physical experiments may include replications and be subject to censoring due to equipment limitations or contextual constraints, and such datasets can be large, posing a scalability challenge for standard Gaussian process inference. Motivated by a real-world industrial research study, we develop a Gaussian process modeling framework that efficiently analyzes large replicated and censored data. Our approach integrates a Vecchia approximation for computational scalability with a likelihood-based formulation that fully exploits replication and rigorously incorporates information from censored observations, analogous to exact simulation from truncated distributions. Through experiments on synthetic data and a real case study from industrial research, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields improved predictive accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches, making it well suited for large-scale applications with structured replication and incomplete data.
picks.why: Combines Vecchia approximation with a likelihood accounting for censoring and replication to scale Gaussian process regression to large industrial datasets.

picks.title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case
picks.abstract: Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator's press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market's initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. Thresholds tuned for the F1 score approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.
picks.why: An interaction-aware scoring framework for FDIC-assisted bank acquisitions performs no better than simple logistic/ridge baselines once properly cross-validated, a useful negative result.

picks.title: AcupunctureBench: A Multimodal Benchmark for Evaluating Generative Models in the Acupuncture Domain
picks.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in the field of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), standardized benchmark evaluations for TCM have gradually emerged. Acupuncture is a crucial component of TCM. However, existing evaluation benchmarks are lacking in this domain. To address this gap, this paper proposes AcupunctureBench, the first independently constructed large-scale multimodal benchmark for the acupuncture domain, covering text, image, and video modalities. The AcupunctureBench spans multidimen sional knowledge in acupuncture, including acupuncture theory, meridians and acupoints, clinical reasoning, TCM syndromes, and practical acupoint operation. To achieve large-scale construction while ensuring medical professionalism, this work designs a human-machine collaborative data construction pipeline and proposes efficient deduplication strategies to reduce redundant samples, while extensively adopting data synthesis to mitigate data leak age risks. AcupunctureBench contains a total of 58,526 question samples and 1,216 video samples, covering multiple task types including objective questions, subjective question answering, case analysis, image understanding, image reasoning, and video understanding. Based on this benchmark, this paper evaluates 14 large language models, 14 large multimodal models, and 4 video foundation models, and further releases the first dedicated evaluation website for the acupuncture domain.
picks.why: AcupunctureBench introduces the first large multimodal benchmark for evaluating LLMs and vision models on acupuncture knowledge and image/video reasoning.

picks.title: Predictability over Volatility: When simple strategies help households save on fuel
picks.abstract: What reasonable strategies can households use to save on gasoline or diesel purchases under different pricing functions? We assess basic strategies households might employ under a simplified model of a 10-gallon tank, fixed fuel consumption between refill opportunities, and price changes at each opportunity to refill. Purchases always fill the tank, and if the tank is empty, it must be refilled regardless of price. We explore three strategy types: price-independent (filling once the tank is below a specific level), price-dependent (filling when the price is below the last n days or their average), and mixed (filling only below a set level, and then only when the price is below the last n days or their average). We construct price functions from the nearest-in-time US weekly averages of regular gasoline and diesel, filling in higher-frequency values with a smoothing spline, linear interpolation, and random draws from normal and uniform distributions based on national averages. Additional simulations are built using Brownian motion. Together, these pricing models span a wide range of volatilities. We find that price-independent strategies are effective for the spline and linear functions, which have low volatility, while price-dependent strategies are effective for the normal and uniform distributions, which are highly volatile. Brownian motion, despite its mid-range volatility, admits no effective strategy. Our findings suggest that the predictability of price movements, whether prices trend or revert toward a stable level, matters more for household strategies than overall volatility: the random walk is volatile in the middle of our range yet offers households no usable signal. Policymakers can therefore assist households by addressing how prices move from day to day, not only the retail prices they face.
picks.why: A simulation study finds that simple fill-up strategies help households save on fuel mainly when prices are predictable, while a pure random walk offers no usable signal.
